# Summary

This report documents a working exposure-linkage pipeline for Freiburg im Breisgau. Satellite land surface
temperature, satellite vegetation, classified land cover and terrain are processed into a hexagonal grid,
quality-screened, gap-filled with a validated method, and linked to a simulated cohort of 500 children over
exposure windows of 7, 30 and 365 days before each child's examination date. The output is a single DuckDB
database with full provenance on every value, 19 automated integrity tests, and a demonstrated incremental
update procedure.

The cohort is simulated; **all environmental data are real**.

```{r headline}
h <- qry("SELECT COUNT(*) AS hexagon_weeks FROM lst_weekly")
s <- qry("SELECT source, COUNT(*) AS n FROM lst_weekly GROUP BY source ORDER BY source")
data.frame(
  Finding = c("Satellite gaps are seasonal and spatially clustered",
              "Ignoring gaps biases annual exposure",
              "Gap-filling method selected on pre-specified rule",
              "Satellite tracks ground-measured weather",
              "Elevation confounds the green–heat relationship",
              "Exposure window determines what is measured",
              "Lower socioeconomic position, hotter and less green"),
  Result = c("14.4% of hexagon-weeks missing; 46% in October, 0.9% in August; 26.5% missing in populated hexagons vs 22.9% elsewhere",
             "Annual exposure overestimated by 1.43 °C on average, in the same direction for nearly every child",
             "Climatology-plus-anomaly, cold-season RMSE 1.66 °C on withheld pixels",
             "Deseasonalised correlation with DWD station Freiburg r = 0.82",
             "Apparent cooling per 10 pp green falls 45% after adjustment (−0.74 to −0.40 °C)",
             "Exam month explains 92% of 7-day exposure; location explains 63% of 365-day exposure",
             "−0.22 °C annual LST and +3.6 pp green per 1 SD higher SES")
) |> show("Headline results", 3)
```

# Background and objective

Environmental epidemiology in child cohorts needs exposure values attached to individual participants at
individual dates. The practical obstacle is rarely the statistical model; it is that satellite records are
incomplete, that the incompleteness is not random, and that exposure must be defined over a window that
matches the hypothesised mechanism.

The objective here was to build the full chain end to end for one city, document every decision, and show
that the result can be maintained when new data arrive. Freiburg was chosen because it spans 195 m on the
Rhine valley floor to 1,283 m in the Black Forest within a single municipality, which makes terrain
confounding visible rather than hypothetical.

## Data sources

```{r sources}
data.frame(
  Source = c("MODIS MOD11A2 v061", "Sentinel-2 L2A", "ESA WorldCover 2021",
             "OpenStreetMap", "Copernicus DEM GLO-30", "DWD station 01443",
             "OSM administrative boundary"),
  Variable = c("Land surface temperature, 8-day composite, 1 km",
               "NDVI, summer median, 10 m",
               "Land cover, 10 m",
               "Parks, forest, water features",
               "Elevation, 30 m",
               "Daily air temperature (Tmax, Tmean)",
               "Municipal boundary"),
  Use = c("Heat exposure 2021–2024", "Vegetation greenness",
          "Green, built-up, cropland, water shares",
          "Independent green comparison; park access",
          "Terrain confounder", "External validation",
          "Study area definition")
) |> show("Input data", 0)
```

## Analytical grid

The city (152.9 km²) was tiled with 204 hexagons of 1 km². Hexagons are preferred to squares because every
neighbour shares an edge at equal centroid distance, which avoids the diagonal-neighbour ambiguity of a
square lattice. Edge hexagons are retained with an `inside_frac` weight; land-cover shares are computed over
the within-city portion only. Applying this weighting changed the citywide built-up share from 13.8% to 16.4%
— the unweighted figure had diluted dense edge hexagons with area outside the municipality.

# Methods

## Quality screening of satellite temperature

MODIS pixels were accepted only where the QC bitfield indicated good quality or an LST error below 2 K
(mandatory QA 0, or 1 with error flag ≤ 1). Pixels failing this were set to missing rather than retained with
a warning flag, on the basis that a flagged value propagates silently into a weekly mean.

A hexagon-week was treated as observed only if **at least 50% of the hexagon area** had valid pixels. Without
this rule, a hexagon mean could be computed from a single clear corner and would not represent the hexagon.
The threshold was fixed before results were examined.

## Gap diagnosis

```{r gap-table}
show(data.frame(
  Window = c("7 days", "30 days", "365 days"),
  `No data at all` = c("50 children (10.0%)", "3 children (0.6%)", "0"),
  `Coverage below 50%` = c("19.6%", "15.0%", "0%"),
  `Worst quarter` = c("Q4: 34.9%", "Q4: 37.2%", "—"),
  check.names = FALSE),
  "Exposure-window completeness before gap-filling", 1)
```

```{r f5}
fig("F5_gaps_by_month.png", "Missing hexagon-weeks by month")
```

```{r f6}
fig("F6_gaps_cold_map.png", "Cold-season data loss by hexagon")
```

Gaps concentrate between October and February and fall more heavily on the dense city core than on the
forested uplands. Hexagons containing cohort children lost 26.5% of cold-season weeks against 22.9% for
hexagons without children. Two mechanisms are plausible and cannot be separated with these data: radiation
fog pooling on the valley floor, and more frequent QC rejection of mixed urban pixels. Either way the
missingness is informative with respect to the study population, which is the reason gap-filling was
validated rather than assumed.

## Gap-filling: candidate methods and selection

Three methods were compared:

1. **Climatology** — the hexagon's own mean for that 8-day slot (±1 slot) across all years.
2. **Linear temporal interpolation** — straight line between the nearest observed weeks for that hexagon.
3. **Climatology plus anomaly** — the hexagon's climatology adjusted by the citywide median anomaly for that
   week, taken from hexagons that *were* observed; where a whole week is missing, the anomaly is interpolated
   in time.

Validation withheld 10% of **known** values and compared each method's reconstruction against the truth,
under two withholding schemes: random pixels (scattered cloud) and whole weeks (missing composites). Twenty
replicates per scheme. Critically, climatology was recomputed from the withheld matrix in every replicate, so
no method had sight of the values it was asked to predict.

**Selection rule, fixed in advance:** lowest cold-season RMSE averaged across both schemes. The cold season
is where the real gaps are.

```{r t1}
show(tab("T1_interpolation_validation_v1.1.csv"), "Gap-filling validation (°C), method v1.1")
```

```{r f7}
fig("F7_interpolation_rmse.png", "Reconstruction error on withheld observations")
```

Climatology-plus-anomaly was selected (cold-season mean RMSE 2.79 °C against 3.99 for climatology and 4.22
for linear). Its advantage is large where part of the week was observed — 1.66 °C against 4.27 and 4.47 for
random withheld pixels — because the citywide anomaly carries that week's actual weather. Where an entire
composite is missing, no anomaly can be borrowed and all three methods converge near 3.7–4.0 °C. That is the
honest ceiling of temporal interpolation without an external meteorological source.

## Outlier screening (protocol v1.1)

External station comparison revealed values that internal cross-validation could not detect, including an
LST of −10.0 °C in the station hexagon on 1 November 2023 against an air maximum of 13.8 °C — a cloud top
recorded as ground. The protocol was therefore amended before the database was built.

Each value was expressed as a deviation from its own hexagon's seasonal climatology, then compared with the
citywide median deviation for that week. Values exceeding **4 robust standard deviations** (MAD-based,
σ = 0.93 °C) were flagged, set to missing, refilled, and retained in the provenance field as
`removed_outlier`. Flagged values total 329, or **1.37% of observations** — concentrated in partly cloudy
weeks (33 hexagons on 9 May 2021; 28 on 27 December 2022), consistent with unmasked cloud edges.

The anomaly estimator was simultaneously made robust: median rather than mean across hexagons, and trusted
only when ≥20% of hexagons were observed that week. This removed the large reconstruction errors previously
seen in sparse weeks such as 2 February 2021 (62 of 650 pixels valid).

```{r t1b}
o <- tab("T1b_outliers_removed.csv")
if (!is.null(o)) {
  o |> count(date, name = "hexagons_flagged") |> arrange(desc(hexagons_flagged)) |> head(8) |>
    show("Dates with most flagged values", 0)
}
```

## Exposure windows

Each composite contributes to a child's window in proportion to the number of days it overlaps that window;
coverage is the fraction of window days with observed data. Because composites tile the calendar exactly,
overlap days must sum to the window length, and this is asserted for all 1,500 child-windows.

Heat is assigned at hexagon level (MODIS pixels are ~1 km). Green exposure is measured in a **300 m buffer**
around the home, following the WHO accessibility indicator, using 10 m data. Each exposure is resolved at the
scale its source supports rather than at a single imposed scale.

# Results

## Effect of gap-filling on child exposures

```{r relink}
show(data.frame(
  Window = c("7 days", "30 days", "365 days"),
  `Children with no prior value` = c(50, 3, 0),
  `Mean change (°C)` = c(-0.01, -0.08, -1.43),
  `Mean absolute change (°C)` = c(0.40, 0.65, 1.45),
  `Largest change (°C)` = c(21.8, 5.48, 4.94),
  check.names = FALSE),
  "Exposure before and after gap-filling", 2)
```

```{r f8}
fig("F8_naive_vs_filled.png", "30-day exposure, gaps ignored versus gaps filled")
```

```{r f9}
fig("F9_hex_timeseries.png", "Observed and filled weeks, 2022, hexagon with most children")
```

The 365-day row is the substantive finding. The mean change (−1.43 °C) is almost identical in magnitude to
the mean absolute change (1.45 °C), meaning nearly every child moved in the same direction. Discarding
incomplete weeks removes winter disproportionately, leaving an annual mean weighted toward summer. Because
gaps are denser in the built-up core, the bias is spatially structured and would inflate an estimated urban
heat island.

For short windows the changes largely cancel (mean −0.01 °C over a mean absolute 0.40 °C) but include
individual corrections up to 21.8 °C, where a cloud-contaminated value had dominated a 7-day mean.

## External validation against a ground station

DWD station 01443 (Freiburg, 48.0232 °N, 7.8343 °E, 236 m) falls in hexagon 107. Daily records for 2021–2023
are complete (1,095 days, no missing maxima).

```{r station}
show(data.frame(
  Metric = c("Raw correlation, LST vs air Tmax",
             "Deseasonalised correlation (monthly anomalies)",
             "Mean LST − Tmax, cold season (48 weeks)",
             "Mean LST − Tmax, warm season (62 weeks)",
             "Residual RMSE, observed weeks (n = 110)",
             "Residual RMSE, filled weeks (n = 25)",
             "Residual mean, filled weeks"),
  Value = c("0.96", "0.82", "−1.9 °C", "+2.9 °C", "2.75 °C", "6.10 °C", "+0.16 °C")
), "Satellite versus ground station, hexagon 107", 2)
```

```{r f10}
fig("F10_station_scatter.png", "Satellite LST against station air temperature")
```

```{r f11}
fig("F11_station_timeseries.png", "Satellite and station temperature, 2021–2023")
```

Raw correlation is high (0.96) but largely reflects the annual cycle and is therefore weak evidence. After
removing month means, agreement remains strong at **r = 0.82**: the satellite identifies which weeks were
unusually warm or cold, not merely which season it was.

The seasonal offsets are physically expected rather than error. In winter the 10:30 surface is **1.9 °C
colder** than the afternoon air maximum, because clear nights cool the ground radiatively and the morning
surface has not recovered; in summer solar heating puts surfaces **2.9 °C above** air temperature. This also
identifies a limitation: MODIS daytime LST is a clear-sky sample, so withheld-clear-week validation is
optimistic relative to true gaps, which occur on cloudy days.

Filled weeks show no systematic bias at the station (**+0.16 °C**), agreeing with the −0.32 °C bias measured
internally, but their scatter is more than twice that of observed weeks (6.10 against 2.75 °C). Inspection
attributes the residual error to entirely missing composites coinciding with unusual weather — late October
2022 reached 23.3 °C and mid-December 2022 was below freezing at the station, neither recoverable from
neighbouring weeks.

## Terrain as a confounder

```{r t3}
show(tab("T3_elevation_confounding.csv"), "Summer LST regressed on green share, with and without elevation")
```

```{r f12}
fig("F12_elevation_hex.png", "Elevation per hexagon, with cohort homes")
```

Green share and elevation correlate at r = 0.55 across hexagons: the Black Forest is both green and high.
Adjusting for elevation reduces the apparent cooling per 10 percentage points of green from **−0.74 °C to
−0.40 °C, a 45% reduction**, while R² rises from 0.52 to 0.77.

The fitted elevation coefficient, **−0.71 °C per 100 m**, is close to the environmental lapse rate of
approximately 0.65 °C per 100 m. That the model recovers a known physical quantity it was not given is
reassuring about the specification.

One qualification deserves emphasis. Cohort homes span only 199–375 m, because built-up land is confined to
the valley floor; the 45% attenuation is therefore identified largely from unpopulated forest hexagons where
no child lives. Within the cohort, terrain contributes roughly 1.2 °C of variation. The practical conclusion
is unchanged — any green–heat analysis in this city must condition on terrain — but the limited overlap
between the exposure contrast and the study population is itself a design finding.

## What an exposure window measures

```{r t4}
show(tab("T4_when_vs_where.csv"), "Variance in LST exposure explained by time versus place", 2)
```

```{r f13}
fig("F13_windows_when_where.png", "The same children under three exposure windows")
```

For a 7-day window, examination month explains 92% of variance in exposure and hexagon explains 1%. For a
365-day window this reverses: 63% is explained by hexagon. The 7- and 365-day exposures correlate at only
0.08, so for an individual child they are close to independent quantities.

This has direct design consequences. A short window answers questions about acute heat before assessment; a
long window answers questions about the residential environment. Comparing children on an unadjusted 7-day
exposure is largely comparing their appointment dates. Residual time dependence at 365 days (R² = 0.36)
reflects genuine interannual variation, visible as the upward drift through 2022.

## Equity gradient

```{r t6}
show(tab("T6_equity.csv"), "Environmental exposure per 1 SD higher socioeconomic position", 4)
```

```{r f14}
fig("F14_equity.png", "Exposure by socioeconomic tertile")
```

Standard errors are clustered by hexagon. Built-up share is a hexagon-level variable and the 500 children
occupy 80 hexagons, so the number of independent spatial observations is far below the number of children.
Models are deliberately unadjusted for built-up share and elevation: these are the pathways through which
the inequality arises, and conditioning on them would remove the quantity of interest.

Per standard deviation of higher socioeconomic position, children experience **0.22 °C lower annual surface
temperature**, **3.6 percentage points more green** within 300 m and **0.026 higher NDVI**. By tertile, the
lowest group lives 0.4 °C warmer with 36% green nearby against 43% for the highest.

The informative null is park access. 88% of children have a public green space of at least 0.5 ha within
300 m, and this varies little by socioeconomic position (85–91%, p = 0.20). In this city inequality is not
about the presence of a nearby green space but about how much greenery surrounds the home. An
access-only indicator would have reported no inequality where a quantity-based indicator finds a clear
gradient.

## Recovery of a known parameter

Socioeconomic position was simulated with a specified dependence on built-up share, giving a true
standardised slope of −0.447. The analysis was then asked to recover it.

```{r t5}
show(tab("T5_truth_recovery.csv"), "Single-cohort recovery of the simulated parameter", 3)
show(tab("T5b_coverage.csv"), "Replication over 500 simulated datasets", 3)
```

```{r f15}
fig("F15_coverage.png", "Sampling distribution of the estimated slope across 500 replications")
```

In the primary cohort the estimate was −0.363 with a clustered 95% interval of −0.436 to −0.290, which
**excludes** the true value. Rather than reseed the simulation, the estimator was evaluated across 500
replications. The mean estimate was **−0.447**, identical to the planted value, and interval coverage was
98.6% (naive) and 97.6% (clustered) against a nominal 95%.

The estimator is therefore unbiased with slightly conservative intervals, and the primary cohort fell in the
0.6% tail of the sampling distribution. Clustering had little effect here because the simulated individual
noise was independent within hexagons; with genuine neighbourhood-level correlation the correction would be
substantial, and it is retained for that reason.

# Database and maintenance

## Structure

```{r db-structure}
qry("SELECT table_name AS \"Table\", estimated_size AS \"Rows\"
     FROM duckdb_tables() ORDER BY table_name") |>
  show("Tables in db/freiburg_exposure.duckdb", 0)
```

Seven tables under composite primary keys. `lst_weekly` is keyed on (hex_id, date), making a duplicate
hexagon-week a constraint violation rather than a silent double count, and `lst_filled` is declared NOT NULL
so a gap cannot be stored. Both constraints were verified by attempting the violation.

Every temperature row carries its `source` (observed, filled or removed outlier), the `method_version` that
produced it and a `run_id` resolving to an entry in `run_log`. Any value in the database can be traced to the
run that created it, and an analyst can restrict to observed values alone.

```{r provenance}
qry("SELECT year(date) AS Year, source AS Source, COUNT(*) AS n
     FROM lst_weekly GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL") |>
  show("Provenance of every stored temperature value", 0)
```

## Incremental update

```{r runlog}
qry("SELECT run_id, run_type, period_start, period_end, n_lst_rows, description
     FROM run_log ORDER BY run_id") |>
  show("Pipeline run log", 0)
```

The 2024 composites were used to exercise the update path. New files land in a staging directory and pass a
quality gate before ingestion: identical raster geometry (650 cells), dates on the 8-day calendar for their
own year, and no date already present. Only then are hexagon means computed, the same 50% rule applied, and
the **same outlier threshold reused** rather than re-estimated from the new data.

All inserts occur in a single transaction. The procedure is idempotent: re-running it reports that nothing is
new rather than duplicating rows.

```{r update-summary}
show(data.frame(
  Check = c("New composites ingested", "Status of new weeks",
            "New rows by provenance", "Outlier threshold",
            "Outliers flagged in 2024", "Rows from run 1 modified",
            "Children requiring recomputation", "Integrity tests after update"),
  Result = c("46 weeks, 9,384 hexagon-weeks",
             "40 usable, 5 mostly cloud, 1 missing composite (26 Dec 2024)",
             "7,719 observed, 1,478 filled, 187 removed",
             "0.95 °C, frozen from existing data",
             "187 (2.0%, against 1.4% for 2021–2023)",
             "None (verified by count and checksum)",
             "0 — all examinations fall in 2022–2023",
             "19 of 19 passed")
), "Incremental update, run 2", 0)
```

2024 was flagged at a higher rate (2.0%) than the baseline period (1.4%) under an unchanged threshold,
indicating more partly cloudy weeks with unmasked cloud edges rather than any change in rule. This is the
kind of drift a monitoring system should surface rather than absorb.

## Automated integrity tests

Nineteen assertions run against the database before and after any update: one row per hexagon-week; the grid
complete against the composite inventory; no null filled values; only permitted source labels; observed
values bit-identical to their raw inputs; every removed outlier present in the outlier log; every row
resolving to a logged run; temperatures within −40 to 70 °C; land-cover shares within [0, 1]; 500 unique
children each in a known hexagon; exactly three windows per child; and each year's composite calendar
starting 1 January in steps of 8 days.

The land-cover assertion failed on first execution, identifying 43 hexagons whose `inside_frac` exceeded 1 by
floating-point rounding. The values were clamped in a logged transaction and the source file corrected so a
rebuild does not reintroduce the defect.

# Limitations

```{r limitations}
show(data.frame(
  Limitation = c("Cohort is simulated",
                 "Clear-sky sampling bias",
                 "Fully missing composites",
                 "Homes sampled uniformly on built-up land",
                 "Spatial autocorrelation not modelled",
                 "Single-city, single-sensor",
                 "External API stability"),
  Consequence = c("The socioeconomic gradient is partly by construction; the exposure data and the pipeline are real",
                  "Validation withheld clear weeks, so reported errors understate error in genuine cloud gaps",
                  "All methods converge near 3.7–4.0 °C; unusual weather in missing weeks is unrecoverable",
                  "Built-up cells include industrial and transport land, so a few homes fall in non-residential areas",
                  "Clustered standard errors address within-hexagon dependence but not continuous spatial correlation",
                  "Thresholds tuned on Freiburg; transfer to flatter or larger cities requires re-validation",
                  "A Planetary Computer change to strict RFC3339 datetimes broke ingestion mid-project"),
  `Planned remedy` = c("Apply to real cohort data under a data-use agreement",
                       "Introduce ERA5-Land reanalysis as a cloud-independent predictor",
                       "Hybrid filling: anomaly where partial coverage exists, reanalysis-informed otherwise",
                       "Weight sampling by the Zensus 2022 100 m population grid",
                       "Fit spatial error or CAR models as sensitivity analysis",
                       "Replicate in a second city with contrasting terrain",
                       "Pin API contracts and assert response schema in the ingestion tests"),
  check.names = FALSE
), "Known limitations and intended remedies", 0)
```

# Reproducibility

Package versions are pinned with `renv`. Numbered scripts run in sequence from study-area definition through
to the database update; downloads are cached so re-runs do not re-fetch. Random seeds are fixed, including
the primary cohort seed, which was set before any result was examined and not subsequently changed.

```{r sessioninfo}
data.frame(
  Component = c("R version", "Database", "Database size", "Pipeline runs logged",
                "Integrity tests", "Period covered", "Figures", "Result tables"),
  Value = c(paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."),
            "DuckDB, 7 tables",
            paste0(round(file.size("db/freiburg_exposure.duckdb") / 1e6, 1), " MB"),
            as.character(qry("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM run_log")$n),
            "19, all passing",
                        with(qry("SELECT MIN(date) AS a, MAX(date) AS b FROM lst_composite"),
                 paste(format(as.Date(a), "%d %b %Y"), "to", format(as.Date(b), "%d %b %Y"))),

            as.character(length(list.files("outputs/figures", pattern = "png$"))),
            as.character(length(list.files("outputs/tables", pattern = "csv$"))))
) |> show("Reproducibility summary", 0)
```
